To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the uneven and changing spatial distributions and temporal sampling of air temperature station networks can introduce network-induced variability of over 0.1°C in estimates of terrestrial average air temperature anomalies; 2) network-induced variability appears to have been substantial during the late-1800s, but has been relatively minor since the 1900's; and 3) the network-induced variability is a function of the spatial distribution of air temperature stations and is independent of the magnitude of the air temperature anomaly

the uneven and changing distributions of air temperature observations can produce unrepresentatively small or large estimates of the spatially averaged change in air temperature over the past century.
network-induced variability can be substantial and that it can be estimated using random and non-random resampling techniques.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of network-induced variability on estimates of terrestrial average air temperature anomalies and the resulting implications for global climate change research.
the spatial and temporal distribution of air temperature stations and how this distribution influences the estimation of terrestrial air temperature anomalies and trend.
the effects of network changes on air temperature anomaly and trend estimates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for the last century, network-induced variability in terrestrial average air temperature anomalies and trend is substantial, and that this variability has been a significant factor in the estimates of air temperature variability and trend that have been published in the literature.
the spatially averaged air temperatures from most networks are reliable, but that the network changes have introduced substantial variability in the estimates of air temperature anomalies.
the spatial variability of air temperature change has been underestimated by the use of historical observation networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the network-induced variability of the spatially averaged air temperatures is not negligible, but is not so large that it overwhelms the signal of global warming.
, in general, the spatial distribution of stations has not been sufficient for the estimation of spatially averaged anomalies, especially in the late 180Os.
network changes are important, but not as important as other sources of uncertainty in air temperature change estimates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
estimates of air temperature anomalies and changes are sensitive to the spatial distribution of stations, especially during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

the network of temperature stations is a critical component in the estimation of terrestrial air temperature variability, and that network variability should be considered when evaluating the magnitude of terrestrial air temperature trends.
network-induced variability is an important consideration in the analysis and interpretation of historical air temperature data sets.
